sections.html: This Rasbora originates from the west coast of Sumatra. It attains a maximum length of about 5 cm. The "hot" name of the species is not only a reminder of the volcanoes in the area where R. vulcanus occurs, but also refers to the bright red-orange colours the males develop during mating. The females are lighter coloured, but they also have an interesting breeding coloration: the anterior centers of the scales become black!

Needs a tight-fitting lid as this species is known to jump. Do not add this fish to a biologically immature tank as it can be susceptible to swings in water chemistry.

Rasbora vulcanus is a small rasbora from West Sumatra, Indonesia, known only from the Batang Si Joontour near the town of Painan. The name refers to the red body colouration of males. It is occasionally sold as R. reticulata or R. cf. reticulata, but the true R. reticulata is a deeper-bodied fish endemic to the island of Nias and lacks the red colouration. Females are pale yellow, and often only the more colourful males are exported.

There have been rumours that the species name was chosen because the fish were originally found in the foothills of Gunung (Mount) Talang, an active volcano in West Sumatra province, Sumatra, Indonesia. It was actually chosen in reference to the red body colouration of males, and although the type specimens were indeed collected from West Sumatra, the locality was the Batang (river) Si Joontour close to the town of Painan, almost 200 km away from Gunung Talang. It is possible that the species is endemic to this region, as records from outside the area are non-existent.
Apparently collected from clear, flowing streams, but this is the only information available to date.
A tank measuring 60 × 38 × 30 cm (~68 litres) is big enough to house a group.

Choice of decor is not especially critical, although the fish tend to show better colouration when maintained in a well-planted set-up with a dark substrate. The addition of some floating plants and driftwood roots or branches to diffuse the light entering the tank also seems to be appreciated and adds a more natural feel. Do not add this fish to a biologically immature tank as it can be susceptible to swings in water chemistry, and be sure to add a tightly-fitting cover as, like most rasboras, it is an accomplished jumper.

• Temperature: 23–26°C
  • pH: seems to do best in weakly acidic to neutral conditions within the range 6.5–7.5
  • Hardness: 2–15 dGH

As with other small Rasbora species it is likely to be a micropredator feeding on small insects, worms, crustaceans and other zooplankton in nature. In the aquarium it will accept dried foods of a suitable size but should not be fed these exclusively. Daily meals of small live and frozen fare such as Daphnia and Artemia along with good quality flakes and granules will result in the best colouration and encourage the fish to come into breeding condition.

This species is very peaceful indeed, making it an ideal resident of the well-furnished community tank. As it places no special demands in terms of water chemistry it can be combined with many of the most popular fish in the hobby including other small cyprinids as well as tetras, livebearers, rainbowfish, anabantoids, catfish and loaches. As always when selecting a compatible community of fish, thorough research is essential and its small adult size must be a consideration. Setting up a community of fishes native to western Sumatra is trickier as exports from the region are sporadic at best.

It's a schooling species by nature and really should be kept in a group of at least 8–10 specimens. Maintaining it in decent numbers will not only make the fish less nervous but will result in a more effective, natural-looking display. Males will also display their best colours as they compete with one another for female attention.

The body of the male is suffused with an orange/red pigmentation which is more intense in dominant individuals, whereas the female is a pale yellow fish, showing only a touch of red in the unpaired fins. Mature females are normally heavier-bodied and a little larger than males. It can be difficult to find females on sale as often only the more colourful, and saleable, males are exported.

Like many small cyprinids it is an egg-scattering, continuous spawner that exhibits no parental care. When the fish are in good condition they will spawn often, and in a densely-planted, mature aquarium small numbers of fry may start to appear without human intervention. However, if you want to increase the yield of fry a slightly more controlled approach is required.

The adult group can still be conditioned together, but one or more long, shallow containers of about 60 × 20 × 20 cm (39 litres) should also be set up and half-filled with water. These should be very dimly lit and the base covered with some kind of mesh of a large enough grade so that the eggs can fall through it but small enough so that the adults cannot reach them. The widely available plastic 'grass'-type matting can also be used and works very well. The water itself should be slightly acidic in pH with a temperature towards the upper end of the range suggested above. A small power filter can be added initially and should be positioned so that the flow is directed down the full length of the tank.

When the adult fish are well-conditioned and the females appear full of eggs, one or two pairs should be introduced to each container. Spawning can be initiated by adding small amounts of cool water every few hours in such a way that the tank is gradually topped up, and by feeding small amounts of live and frozen foods. Spawning usually occurs in the morning and several events will usually occur before a female is spent of eggs.

The adults will eat any eggs they find and are best removed after a couple of days, at which point the power filter should be replaced by a mature sponge-type unit in order to avoid fry being sucked into the mechanism. Incubation is temperature-dependent to an extent but usually takes between 18 and 48 hours, with the young free-swimming 24 to 48 hours later. Initial food should be Paramecium or similar, introducing Artemia nauplii and/or microworm once the fry are large enough to accept them.

Rasbora vulcanus is a close relative of Rasbora reticulata. The latter is found exclusively on the island of Nias and does not occur on Sumatra. R. reticulata can be distinguished best from R. vulcanus by the presence of dark stripes on the outer edges of the caudal fin, which are always lacking in R. vulcanus.

This species was described in 1999 and may still occasionally be seen on sale under the incorrect names R. reticulata or R. cf. reticulata as well as the trade name 'volcano rasbora'. The real R. reticulata is endemic to the small island of Nias off Sumatra's northwestern coast and is virtually inaccessible to fish collectors, so is unlikely to be in the hobby, although it may have been exported on a couple of occasions. It is a deeper-bodied fish and does not exhibit the red colouration seen in R. vulcanus, although both species share a pattern of dark edging to the scales on the body.

Rasbora has long been recognised as a polyphyletic lineage, as noted by Kottelat (1999) amongst others. In 2010 a phylogenetic analysis by Liao et al. suggested a number of changes to improve the taxonomy and erected four new genera containing former members of Rasbora, while Tang et al. (2010) reached differing results and synonymised the new genera plus Boraras and Trigonostigma with Rasbora. R. vulcanus was listed by Liao et al. among the unclassified species, possibly not Rasboras. The type species of Rasbora is R. cephalotaenia.
